guided.title: Overlap test
guided.prompt: Write `overlaps(a, b)` that returns True when two rectangles (dicts with `x`, `y`, `w`, `h`) share any area (touching edges do not count as overlap). Print the results for the pairs (A, B), (A, C), (B, C), one per line, where A is x 0, y 0, 100 by 100; B is x 100, y 0, 100 by 100; C is x 50, y 50, 100 by 100.
hints: Rectangles overlap when they overlap on both axes.
On the x axis: a.x < b.x + b.w and b.x < a.x + a.w.
Combine the x and y tests with and, using strict inequalities.

guided.title: Grid and bounds
guided.prompt: Given `page` (below), print the names of visuals that are off the 1280 by 720 canvas or not on the 40 pixel grid, one per line in list order, formatted as `name: problem` where problem is `off canvas` or `not on grid` (a visual with both problems gets `off canvas` first, then `not on grid`, as two lines).
guided.starter:
CANVAS_W, CANVAS_H, GRID = 1280, 720, 40

def overlaps(a, b):
    return (a["x"] < b["x"] + b["w"] and b["x"] < a["x"] + a["w"]
            and a["y"] < b["y"] + b["h"] and b["y"] < a["y"] + a["h"])

page = [
    {"name": "kpi", "type": "card", "x": 40, "y": 40, "w": 360, "h": 120},
    {"name": "trend", "type": "line", "x": 40, "y": 200, "w": 760, "h": 480},
    {"name": "mix", "type": "bar", "x": 760, "y": 200, "w": 440, "h": 480},
    {"name": "notes", "type": "table", "x": 440, "y": 40, "w": 360, "h": 100},
]

# print the problems
hints: Check each visual's right and bottom edge against the canvas size.
The grid test is value % GRID != 0 for x, y, w and h.
Print f"{name}: off canvas" before f"{name}: not on grid".

guided.title: Contrast check
guided.prompt: Using `contrast(fg, bg)` (given), print `colour ratio verdict` for the foreground colours #1A1A1A, #888888 and #0B3D91 on a #FFFFFF background, with the ratio rounded to 2 decimals and the verdict `pass` for ratios of 4.5 or more, otherwise `fail`, for example `#FF0000 4.0 fail`.
hints: Round the ratio to 2 decimals for printing.

guided.title: Critique a layout (written)
guided.prompt: A page has twelve visuals of equal size in a 4 by 3 grid, all with bright, different colours, and a table of 40 rows in the middle. Slicers are scattered at the corners. Describe the hierarchy problems and redesign the page in words, with the order in which the reader should read it.
guided.solution: Equal sizes and equal colours give the reader no entry point, so nothing is read first. Twelve visuals exceed the working limit of six to eight and compete for attention; the 40-row table in the centre takes the best position for the least useful content. Scattered slicers hide the filter state. A redesign: one row of three KPI cards on the top, with the headline measure top left; below, one large trend chart taking about 40% of the canvas; beside it a bar chart of the main breakdown; slicers in one strip along the top. Move the table to a drill-through page. Use one accent colour for the key series and grey for the rest, so one thing stands out. The reading order is KPI cards, trend, breakdown, then the slicers for exploration.
rubric: Names missing hierarchy: equal size and colour, no entry point.
Reduces the number of visuals and moves detail to drill-through.
Places KPIs top-left, the main chart largest, slicers in one strip.
hints: What does the eye land on first?
How many visuals are too many?
Where would you put the headline number?

Run it on `page` (given) and print each problem on its own line, or `no problems` if the list is empty.

            and a["y"] < b["y"] + b["h"] and b["y"] < a["y"] + a["h"])

independent.title: Theme audit
independent.prompt: A theme has `text`, `background` and a list of `data_colours`. Using `contrast`, print the contrast of the text on the background (2 decimals, `text 11.59`), then for each data colour print `colour ratio ok` where `ok` is `mark` when its contrast with the background is at least 3.0 (a common threshold for graphics) and `weak` otherwise. Use text #333333, background #F5F5F5 and colours #0B3D91, #118DFF, #F2C811, #6B007B in that order.

independent.title: Phone stacking and budget (stretch)
independent.prompt: Given the `page` list (below, with `h` as desktop height) build a phone order sorted by (y, x). Use phone heights: card 80, line 220, bar 220, table 260. Print the order as `name top` lines (top = cumulative height before it) and then `scroll N`. Drop any visual of type `table` first, because tables are left off the phone.
independent.starter:
page = [
    {"name": "kpi", "type": "card", "x": 40, "y": 40},
    {"name": "trend", "type": "line", "x": 40, "y": 200},
    {"name": "mix", "type": "bar", "x": 760, "y": 200},
    {"name": "notes", "type": "table", "x": 440, "y": 40},
    {"name": "kpi2", "type": "card", "x": 440, "y": 100},
]
heights = {"card": 80, "line": 220, "bar": 220, "table": 260}
# phone order and scroll length
independent.solution:
page = [
    {"name": "kpi", "type": "card", "x": 40, "y": 40},
    {"name": "trend", "type": "line", "x": 40, "y": 200},
    {"name": "mix", "type": "bar", "x": 760, "y": 200},
    {"name": "notes", "type": "table", "x": 440, "y": 40},
    {"name": "kpi2", "type": "card", "x": 440, "y": 100},
]
heights = {"card": 80, "line": 220, "bar": 220, "table": 260}
top = 0
for v in sorted((v for v in page if v["type"] != "table"), key=lambda v: (v["y"], v["x"])):
    print(v["name"], top)
    top += heights[v["type"]]
print("scroll", top)

environment.note: Page layout, themes and the phone layout are set in Power BI Desktop (Windows-only, View and Format panes), and a theme JSON can be imported there. Menu names can differ between versions. The graded exercises test the layout rules and colour contrast with plain Python, which runs in the browser.

checks.question: Two visuals have x ranges 0 to 100 and 100 to 200 and the same y range. Do they overlap?
options: Yes, they share the x value 100
No, they only touch at an edge
checks.explanation: Rectangles overlap only if they share area on both axes. Touching edges have no area in common, so the strict inequality in the test returns False.

checks.question: What contrast ratio does WCAG ask for as a minimum for normal text?
checks.explanation: 4.5 is the minimum for normal text; 3.0 is used for large text and graphics. 21 is the maximum, black on white.

checks.question: Which change gives a page a clearer visual hierarchy?
options: Make every visual the same size
Give the key trend the largest area and one accent colour
Use a different bright colour for each visual
Move the slicers to random corners
checks.explanation: Hierarchy comes from size, position, colour contrast and grouping. Equal size and many colours remove the entry point.

checks.question: A phone layout in Power BI Desktop:
options: Copies the visuals into a second report
Rearranges the same page's visuals for a narrow screen, sharing measures and filters
Is created automatically for every page
checks.explanation: The phone layout shows the same visuals, so data and filters are shared, but the author must place them. A page without one is shown as the scaled desktop page.

checks.question: What is the problem with #F2C811 (yellow) on a white background?
options: Yellow is not allowed in themes
Its contrast with white is about 1.6, which is low even for marks and far too low for text
checks.explanation: Marks should reach about 3.0 and small text 4.5; the yellow, at about 1.6 on white, misses both, so it needs a darker background or a darker colour.
